titre: A Few Days With One Eye Closed: The Kitten's Critical Period
accroche: In 1970, Hubel and Wiesel show that an eye closed for a few days, at a precise age, loses almost all hold on the cat's visual cortex.
contenu_vulgarise:
You might think that an eye closed after birth stays intact, ready to be used as soon as it is reopened. David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel's experiments on kittens say the opposite: closing an eye at the right age durably changes what the cortex makes of it.

## The Protocol

The two researchers suture the eyelids of the right eye of young cats, for varying lengths of time and at different ages. Later, they record the activity of cells in the visual cortex and count how many respond to each eye. They had already observed that monocular closure during the first months causes a drop in the number of cells that the closed eye can still influence. The 1970 article asks when this happens.

## A Window That Opens All at Once

Sensitivity to eye closure begins abruptly around the start of the fourth week. It stays high until the sixth or eighth week, then declines, and disappears around the age of three months. A closure of more than a year in an adult cat produces no detectable effect.

During the sensitive window, the effect is fast: closing an eye for three to four days, during the fourth and fifth weeks, is enough to clearly reduce the number of cells drivable by both eyes and the relative weight of the closed eye. Six days produce a drop to a fraction of normal. After three months of deprivation from birth, the share of cells that the eye can influence goes from about 85% to about 7%.

## What Does Not Come Back

Reopening the eye does not fix much: after three months of deprivation, even five years of open eye bring only very limited recovery of cortical physiology, and no obvious recovery of the atrophy of the thalamic relay, even though behavior shows some return of vision. The cells of this relay (the lateral geniculate body) that receive the deprived eye are, moreover, visibly smaller and paler after three or six days of closure.

## What This Shifts

The cat's visual wiring does not set itself on its own: a few days of deprivation are enough to modify it during the sensitive window, and very little can be made up afterward. For the cat, this period is counted in weeks. It also sets a limit on what these experiments allow: they concern cats, and what they say about other species remains a question to be investigated, not an answer.

repere.texte: After three months of monocular deprivation from birth, the proportion of cells in the kitten's visual cortex that the deprived eye can influence goes from about 85% to about 7%.
repere.source: Hubel & Wiesel, The Journal of Physiology, 206(2), 1970

carte.punch: Closing a kitten's eye for a few days is enough to sharply reduce its influence on the cortex.
carte.idee: Hubel and Wiesel (1970): sensitivity to the closure of an eye opens around the kitten's fourth week and disappears around three months. In the adult cat, a year of closure changes nothing.

quiz.question: What do Hubel and Wiesel show when they close a kitten's eye during the sensitive period?
choix: That the effect appears only after more than a year of closure, in kittens as in adults
That a few days are enough to clearly reduce the number of cells the closed eye influences
That the closed eye regains its full weight in the cortex as soon as it is reopened, whatever the age
That the effect is the same in the adult cat as in the kitten, for equal closure duration
quiz.explication: During the fourth and fifth weeks, 3 to 4 days of closure already clearly reduce the number of cells drivable by the closed eye, and 6 days give a fraction of normal. After three months of deprivation, recovery remains very limited even after five years of open eye; in the adult, more than a year of closure has no detectable effect.

quiz_supplementaire.question: At what age does sensitivity to eye closure begin in the kitten?
choix: Around the start of the fourth week
It never begins in the kitten, only in the adult
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text places the abrupt start of this sensitivity around the start of the fourth week, not at birth or after six months, and it does exist in the kitten, unlike the adult.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What becomes of the cells of the lateral geniculate body, the thalamic relay, after several days of eye closure?
choix: They regain normal size as soon as the eye is reopened
They disappear completely and are never found at autopsy
They stay smaller and paler, with no obvious recovery even after five years
They grow larger instead, to compensate for the loss of the closed eye
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that after three months of deprivation, even five years of open eye bring no obvious recovery of the atrophy of the geniculate body.
